verdicts.message: Leaked secret: signing-key: signing-key detected. Treat the value as compromised: it is readable by everyone who has ever had the repository, and deleting the line does not un-publish it. In order — (1) REVOKE it at whatever issued it and issue a replacement, which is the only step that actually closes the exposure; (2) load the replacement at run time from your platform's secret store or the process environment instead of from the tree, so no future value is committable; (3) remove the file or line and add its path to the repository's ignore rules, so it cannot come back; (4) if the value was ever live, purge it from the history as well, since a clone taken before the deletion still carries it. If this is instead a FIXTURE — key material generated for tests and valid nowhere — then the exposure is nil and the fix is to make that legible: generate it in test setup, or keep it under a test-data path, so a reader (and this scan) can tell it from the real thing.

verdicts.message: Rotate the exposed credentials — git history can't be un-committed: Some of these secrets are in git HISTORY: deleting the file does not remove them (the commit persists on every clone, fork and backup). The remediation is to ROTATE each historically-exposed credential and treat it as compromised — not to delete the file. Rewriting history is disruptive and unreliable across existing forks. (Working-tree-only secrets — no commit — can instead be removed from the file and moved to a secret store.) If flagged rows sit in content that is not this repository's own authored code — tool-emitted artifacts, recorded scanner output, wholesale-vendored third-party files — declare that provenance in .gitattributes (`path/** linguist-generated` or `linguist-vendored`): this scanner honors the repository's own declarations and stops counting such content, history-anchored rows included, on the next scan. The declaration is a reviewable statement about provenance, not a suppression — never use it on files that carry your own credentials.

verdicts.message: High: npm-missing-minimum-release-age: This .npmrc does not set a minimum release age or sets it too low. Newly published packages can be malicious or unstable. Added in: v11.10 Reference: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-02-18-npm-bulk-trusted-publishing-config-and-script-security-now-generally-available/. This is a semgrep security-AUDIT rule reporting a POLICY that is absent or weaker than its recommendation, not an exploitable defect. Confirm whether the current setting is a deliberate decision for this repository — and apply the change where it is not; where it is (a policy your release process already enforces elsewhere, or one this repository has consciously opted out of), record the decision and leave the configuration as it is.

falseNegatives.reason: `postgres://media_app:<24 alphanumerics>@pg-shared…` fallback connection URI in src/db/pool.ts:9, verified with sed; credentials embedded in a URI were reported by neither secret engine nor SAST (same blind spot as the C# repo's SEC-014).
Punctuated password inside a `mongodb+srv://user:pw@host` URI in the committed .env:4, verified. Missed by D13 and D28.
Unquoted `JWT_SIGNING_SECRET=<64 base64 chars>` in .env.production:3, verified. D13 opens the dotenv family but its name-driven rules need a quoted value; gitleaks did not match either.

`Authorization: Bearer <48-char token>` on both requests of requests/transcoder.http (lines 6, 16), verified. `.http` is not a scanned extension for D13 and gitleaks' authorization rule did not match the unquoted header line.

64-hex HMAC upload-signing secret injected into the browser bundle via Vite `define: { __UPLOAD_SIGNING_SECRET__: JSON.stringify("…") }` (web/vite.config.ts:13), verified present in the built bundle. Missed by all engines; the value sits inside a call, not a name binding.

scoreBands.note: D37 is NotApplicable without SECURITY.md: the scanner does not score the absence of a disclosure policy; recorded as leniency, band kept.

observations: The history-only plant (a Slack bot token added in 0d4ff97 and removed in the next commit) was found at exactly its commit — unlike the C# repo's history plant, which was a punctuated password.

Typed vendor formats were all found (ghp_, rk_live_, SG., xoxb-, hooks.slack.com, AKIA pairs incl. one in a // comment, PEM and service-account keys); every miss is a credential without a vendor prefix: passwords in postgres:// and mongodb+srv:// URIs, an unquoted dotenv signing secret, a bearer token in a .http file, an HMAC secret in a Vite define.

SEC-003 (literal fallback of process.env.JWT_SIGNING_SECRET) was found only by the SAST secret-env-literal-fallback rule, not by either secret engine; the same rule did not fire on the identical `env.X ?? "literal"` shape in src/storage/objectStore.ts (found there by the AKIA signature) or src/db/pool.ts (a `config.x ??` shape).

Trap resistance 22/23: the Stripe publishable key, Firebase web config + VAPID public key, AWS documentation pair, expired README token, test-only Ed25519 key, __fixtures__ webhook URL, SRI and lock-file hashes, placeholders and Compose interpolation were all left alone; only secret-manager UUIDs under signing-key-shaped names were reported.

The off-theme rows were useful during authoring: the 'thin authorization enforcement' row led to a real spoofable-owner-header weakness being fixed (00c3619). After the fix centralised the check, the same row reported 'only 1 place' — a call-site count that penalises centralisation.
